posts.author: ErichRose
posts.content_md:
I am looking to save some money and build my own laser power meter. Has anyone built the one described in J. Iovine's book? Its all Radio Shack parts and appears fairly straight forward.

Or are there other designs you might suggest?

posts.author: JohnFP
posts.content_md: Well, I am not sure how much you want to spend and how much research and time you want to put into a meter, but Jeff Blyth turned me on to this one and I simply love it. It has the capability to being set to almost any wavelength. It can measure the beam strength out of the laser up to 1 watt and can measure the expanded beam strength at the plate down to .5uW (not milli but micro). It has a small profile and is hand held, thusly can be placed almost anywhere. For $335 US it will be a meter you will use for many years and can grow into if you decide to go with a different wavelenght or up your power.

posts.author: Cristiano_Perrucci
posts.content_md:
> **ErichRose:** I am looking to save some money and build my own laser power meter. Has anyone built the one described in J. Iovine's book? Its all Radio Shack parts and appears fairly straight forward.Or are there other designs you might suggest?

Here's my home made power meter i'm currently using for optical measurements. It's a standard DC coupled TIA followed by a variable gain amplifier in order to linearize the photodiode responsivity for each wavelegth. Mine is tuned for 488,532,633,670nm

The circuit has been tested up to 70mW @488nm with very good results.Over this level of power I think non-linearity effects of the photodiode might affect the measure itself.

For the first prototype I used a 0.5cm^2 silicon fotodiode, multiplying the readout by two, one can get the density power per cm^2. A Excel sheet calculates energy required thus exposure time, doing the dirty job for me.

Unfortunally the diagram was written in Italian for the Italian Laser & Holography ML.

![Image](http://digilander.libero.it/crispers/powmet.jpg)

posts.author: holography4fun
posts.content_md:
The best idea would be using a solar cell as detector.

Use a diffuser infront of the solar cell, to distribute the intensity evenly in the solar cell.

Then use a POWER METER and caliberate it.

posts.author: ErichRose
posts.content_md:
Cristiano, thank you for the diagram. It looks a bit more complicated than the one in Iovine's book but that may be just because it's drafted by hand. 

Ed, those books are hard to find. The Radio Shack web site search engine will not find them. 

The other issue I am seeing with all these hand made units is the need to calibrate. At least if I am to make use of existing exposure charts I will have to find another calibrated meter to set the home built one to. All my lasers are old and I have no idea what they are currently putting out. I guess it's time to make some friends at the university.

posts.author: Joe Farina
posts.content_md:
Unfortunately, those books don't seem to be available at the stores, either. That's a shame, because they are excellent (I have many of them). Radio Shack seems to be moving away from the needs of the electronics enthusiast. They seem to moving (more and more) towards "consumer products" in the pejorative sense.

Anyway, for an exposure meter, I recommend the "age-old" analog voltmeter (with a cadmium sulfide photocell, i.e., a photoresistor). I *think* the cadmium sulfide cells are still available from Radio Shack (!) The only problem is that it's hard to find an analog voltmeter with a lot of resistance ranges (for varying light levels). Having the needle (analog as opposed to digital) is really a necessity for this kind of work in my opinion. The one I use has a large needle and 6 resistance ranges:

[http://www.tequipment.net/ProtekA450.asp](http://www.tequipment.net/ProtekA450.asp) 

As for measuring laser power, in my opinion there is no alterantive: a reliable, calibrated one is needed. I use the LaserCheck as mentioned above.

> **holography4fun:** The best idea would be using a solar cell as detector.Use a diffuser infront of the solar cell, to distribute the intensity evenly in the solar cell.Then use a POWER METER and caliberate it.

I've never seen solar cell as power meters detector in the visible region of the spectrum. On the other hand , silicon PDs are widely used from 400 up to 1600nm.

I think the problem of SCs is bandwidth (a non problem for CW sources) , linearity and dinamic range.
